subtopic: JOB VACANCY SURVEY-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
JOB VACANCY SURVEY-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I request unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent necessity. I hope Your Honour will allow me the necessary minute to give a brief, succinct but necessary preamble.
Early in 1967 the Bureau of Statistics, now Statistics Canada, projected a large-scale program of occupational job vacancy surveys for the use of business, industry, the federal and provincial governments, and universities. The main purpose of the survey is to provide a measure of the demand for labour in Canada. The data can be used to assist in formulating manpower training, immigration policies, educational courses, and the development of career planning. Late in 1969-this is my last sentence, Mr. Speaker-the program began to operate. In the past two years Statistics Canada has supplied such data to the Department of Manpower and Immigration on a regular basis but has withheld this data from the provincial governments and the public. I would like to propose, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House orders Statistics Canada and the responsible ministers to cease the suppression of this $3 million, 106-man job vacancy survey and immediately publish the survey together with all relevant and incidental material.

maintopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOTIVE PACT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOTIVE PACT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 which provides that in cases of urgent and pressing necessity a motion may be moved if unanimous consent is given. I should say, Mr. Speaker, that I have taken care to distribute copies of this motion to the House leaders and I expect that, given the urgency of the matter, I will get unanimous consent and no debate will be necessary.
The matter of urgent and pressing necessity arises out of statements made yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in which the minister suggested that a ceiling is to be placed on the level of Canadian automotive production. This position flatly contradicts the second stated purpose of the Canada-United States Automotive Agreement, Article 1(b), which asserts Canada is to have a "fair and equitable" share in the future growth of the total automotive market of the two countries.
Therefore, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask leave to move, seconded by the member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House reasserts its commitment to Article 1(b) of the Canada-United States Automotive Agreement which reads:
"The liberalization of United States and Canadian automotive trade in respect of tariff barriers and other factors tending to impede it, with a view to enabling the industries of both countries to participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of the two countries".

First of all, can the parliamentary secretary tell me the real purpose in granting this tax exemption? Is it a tax concession to encourage production, or a tax exemption to encourage the removal of pollution? This question must be answered before we can look at the clause in its proper perspective.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: The removal of the excise tax on pollution control equipment used in processing and manufacturing is consistent with the policy of the government to encourage production and manufacturing, and hence employment. It is not specifically an incentive directed at pollution control so much as an incentive to manufacturers and producers to upgrade their facilities and thus have the result of reducing pollution.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
In considering what the government has tried to accomplish in this regard within the past year and a half or two years, we have to look at the over-all structure of the two areas. We must determine whether this incentive will produce a climate in which manufacturers will be encouraged to undertake the type of pollution control that we would all like to see them undertake. I am rather amazed, after reading the correspondence that has been exchanged between the Minister of Finance and the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, that the government has been so little concerned about granting a similar type of concession to municipalities. If we look at this from the point of view that a manufacturer is going to obtain some type of tax concession, then possibly we would argue against it. However, I point out that the relevant part of the clause reads:
-machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers-
It appears, therefore, that manufacturers can import this machinery without paying this tax provided it is used for "detection, measurement, prevention, treatment, reduction of or removal of pollutants."
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities tried to elicit information from the government on this matter. I am sure all hon. members have copies of this correspondence in their files. On June 25 last the Federation wrote, and I quote:
Under the present Excise Tax Act, municipalities are granted some specific exemptions for anti-pollution equipment. However, this list of items is limited and there is still much anti-pollution equipment such as incinerators, recycling systems and crushers on which municipalities must pay tax. It is our interpretation that under the terms of the new exemption municipal government will be the only institution paying federal sales tax on anti-pollution equipment.
The reply by the Minister of Finance on July 26 is along the lines of comments made yesterday by the hon. member for Edmonton West when he was speaking on this clause. Here is what the minister wrote, in part:
Were we to extend this exemption, the description of the equipment that would qualify for this exemption would be a complicated question. For example, incinerators, though they may reduce waste, also cause air pollution; regarding crushers, they have no other utility than to facilitate the transportation of wastes.
A further letter from the Federation dated September 15 spelled out in detail why it thought municipalities should be exempted under the provisions of this bill. In particular it asked the minister:
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
Exactly what are these definitional problems that appear to be so complex for municipalities but which you seemed not to face or were able to resolve in the case of manufacturers and producers?
That is the type of question someone on the government side must answer. If the problems were so complex so far as manufacturers and producers were concerned, how could they be resolved in their case but not in the case of municipalities? There should be no difficulty resolving the same types of problems with respect to municipalities.
In his further reply of October 22, the Minister of Finance tried to deal with this matter of how to distinguish between pollution control machinery that should be exempted and that which should not be exempted. The last paragraph of that letter reads:
You may have in mind the exemption that has been in the law for some years for equipment to carry refuse or waste from production machinery. Neither this exemption nor the exemption announced in June extends to motor vehicles.
It appears that we are simply going round and round the block. Away back on April 22, Mayor Ivan Dent presented a brief from the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to the government, and in that brief commended the government for trying to do something about pollution control. But the position still exists that municipalities which purchase pollution control equipment do not receive the same consideration as manufacturers and producers.
Yesterday the hon. member for Edmonton West, speaking on this problem which was raised by myself and my colleague from Kootenay West, as recorded at page 10,643 of Hansard said:
To say that municipalities and provinces should not have to pay sales tax on machinery or apparatus used in the production of goods is not feasible.
Then, he went on to say:
-I do not think this is the place to do it-
He meant that such an exemption should not be made in this bill. But he failed to explain why municipalities should not be given the same consideration as producers and manufacturers. It seems as though we are just playing with words. Municipalities are a basic ingredient of our democratic society. They have to answer first so far as the public are concerned. They are trying to bring about pollution control, but the government says they are not to receive the same consideration as producers and manufacturers. We also know, Mr. Chairman, that in different areas of the country many apartment with incinerators do not receive consideration, and I am sure other hon. members will have something to say about that. It seems to me that our pollution control measures must be consistent, and we must also be consistent in our treatment of municipalities. Usually this government regards them as fairly credible bodies-especially when they want to foist more education costs on them-but now when it has a chance of doing something for these municipalities the government is found wanting.
I would therefore move:
That clause 4 of Bill C-260 be amended by inserting in line 29 on page 2, after the word "producers", also in line 36 on page 2, after the word "producers", and also in line 6 on page 3, after the word "producers", the following words, "or municipalities".

the pith of my submission. The argument that private members cannot move amendments because they upset the balance or ways and means is a form of words that really does not apply any more in these matters.

If it were the imposition of a tax we would be in trouble if a private member tried to move it, but I submit that the rulings made by the Chair in recent weeks are correct and that this amendment is in order and should be put.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in recent weeks on Bill C-259 we were dealing with rather exceptional circumstances in that the ways and means motion had been supplemented by a particular motion of the House regularizing a variety of proceedings that had occurred before. Mr. Chairman, at some time in the past the amendment in this bill was considered to be an appropriate one. Sometimes I find myself on the side of the hon.

member for Edmonton West, since the party forming the government has to take a middle course between the two opposition parties. I really could not put the argument much better than he put it last night when he advanced the reasons for declining to exempt all municipal purchases of pollution abatement equipment or, for that matter, other equipment from the federal sales tax.
The exemption that we are seeking here recognizes that the cost of pollution abatement is a necessary cost of production. It is consistent with existing exemptions in the bill for production equipment. That is the reason for the exemption. In our thinking we have advanced to the appreciation that the cost of pollution abatement equipment is a proper cost of production, and that is why we want this particular amendment to go forward.
The hon. member for Kootenay West was quite correct. Materials purchased by municipalities for sewage systems, drainage systems and sewage treatment plants are exempt. Of course, that includes a large part of the equipment purchased by municipalities in this area.
The argument presented by the hon. member for Moose Jaw that municipalities will remain the only bodies subject to the payment of sales tax when buying pollution abatement equipment is most fallacious. This provision applies as well to service agencies, transport companies, and so on, and is by no means restricted to municipalities. The exemption here and the exemption that will be brought forward is to apply to production equipment. That is the extent to which the government is prepared to go at this particular point with the amendment to the Act.
I might say that the hon. member's amendment would not be particularly helpful to any municipality unless that municipality happens to be engaged in production. That will be the effect of the amendment if one reads the section as it now is. I really do not feel, therefore, that he would achieve at all what he thought he would by presenting the amendment which has been accepted by the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, first, may I commend to the hon. member who moved the amendment the reading at this time of Part XII of Schedule III which deals with municipalities. He is faced with a procedural problem in that this particular part of that schedule is not included in the amending bill and, therefore, he may not move an amendment to it. Part XII of Schedule III exempts the payment by municipalities of tax on culverts, firefighting equipment, and so on. Subparagraph (e) of section 1 reads:
(e) goods for use as part of sewerage and drainage systems and. for the purposes of this exemption, any agency operating a sewerage or drainage system for or on behalf of a municipality may be declared by the Minister to be a municipality.
Section 2 says that articles and materials for use exlcu-sively in the manufacture of the tax exempt goods mentioned in the section I have just referred to are included.
The amendment that the hon. member moved comes under Part XIII of Schedule III. Part XIII is headed, "Production Equipment, Processing Materials and Plans". It deals with that category of industry and not with municipalities. Although I sympathize with what the hon. member is trying to do, I would find it difficult to bring
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
his amendment under this heading. It seems to me that what should have been done to answer the prayer of the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities is to amend Part XII of the act. I know Mayor Dent of the city of Edmonton and I know that the city is not in any way engaged in the production of goods. After all, this amendment would not help municipalities in any way. The section, if amended, would read:
(b) machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers or municipalities, for use by them directly in the detection-
The key words come at the end of the paragraph and are, "attributable to the manufacture or production of goods". Those words have not been included for dressing up the subsection. I do not know what municipalities are producing goods and that is where the limitation would come in. The amendment would not help municipalities to deal with other aspects of the pollution for which they are responsible. It seems to me, as I pointed out yesterday, that there is a far better way of giving municipalities direct assistance. We should not force them to buy tax exempt equipment which is irrelevant to their purposes. Actually, under a program of forgivable loans, we ought to give municipalities a real incentive to get into the sewage treatment business. Not only would municipalities gain advantages that way from forgivable loans, but they could improve their employment situation as well as their pollution standards. They would also, by reason of the provisions of Part XII of the act, not have to pay any sales tax whatever on any equipment used in these sewage systems, and the same would apply to equipment used to control air pollution.
I do not know whether the hon. member thinks that the production of electricity is the production of goods. I know that the city of Edmonton could clean up a great deal of its municipal electric production plants. The responsibility there comes under another aspect, and the question of sales tax is not involved. I, myself, cannot support this amendment at this particular time, since its effect will be limited to the production of goods manufactured by municipalities.

Mr, Chairman, about clause 4 concerning pollution, I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to the minister whether or not the government really intends to help municipalities fight pollution.
I should also like to know whether or not, the government is considering any help to industries that have great problems with water pollution, because some of them have had to pay significant fines for violating antipollution rules.
But if municipalities are exempted from the tax on certain materials used in the construction of facilities designed to control pollution, we should also exempt from this tax manufacturers who, by using water, contribute to pollution.
A great number of Canadians are living on lake shores. Some reside there the year round. They are faced with the problem of water pollution because inspectors visit them and condemn all their facilities. They force these citizens to take measures against pollution and this costs thousands of dollars. I ask whether it would not be possible to include in some clause a provision to the effect that citizens residing along lake shores, in camps for instance, be exempt from the tax on building materials, so as to contribute to pollution control.
Provincial governments now send inspectors to visit facilities and they condemn several of these. So, citizens have to spend considerable amounts to fight pollution.

If the government really wants to fight pollution, citizens and corporations should at least be exempted from paying the tax on building materials, if there is no other way to assist them through grants, for instance, which might be too costly. Citizens should be exempted from payment of that tax, particularly major industries which have to spend millions of dollars to fight pollution. I make this request of the minister who said a little while ago that several things would not come under the tax.
I therefore ask whether citizens and corporations I have mentioned will be exempted from payment of the tax on building materials.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT

Mr. Chairman, there is nothing in the bill to eliminate the sales tax currently imposed on construction materials, or is it the intention of the government to introduce such an exemption at the present time. The question of that exemption has been forcibly brought to the attention of the government on numerous occasions by many organizations and associations as well as by members of this House. However, if and when a decision is made on that, it will be announced by the minister in a budget statement.
This particular bill does not embrace that concept. The same situation applies, of course, to the total exemption of purchases by municipalities from sales tax. This is a position that is argued by the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. It has been argued by members of this House. However, a decision in this regard is a matter of a budgetary nature and can only be dealt with in the usual way. This particular bill does not encompass that.
With regard to the concern of the hon. member for Compton in connection with processing and manufacturing industries, yes, clause 4(2) of the bill proposes to exempt and I quote:
machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them directly in the detection, measurement, prevention, treatment, reduction or removal of pollutants to water, soil or air-
On that point, Mr. Chairman, I am able to assure the hon. member that this particular bill does comply with his requirements.
In speaking to the amendment that is before the House, I should specifically point out to hon. members that they will have a bit of nonsense if they accept the amendment. The amendment the hon. member really wants to make will, I presume, put an additional classification in Part XII of schedule III to the Excise Tax Act. equipment sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers or municipalities for use by them for exhausting dust and noxious fumes produced by their manufacturing or producing operations;

The amendments he has proposed to the ensuing subclauses of clause 1 of Part XIII would, of course, be equally non-sensical. As I have said, the question is something which is constantly brought to the attention of the government. Up to this point, the government has not

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make my own position clear on this matter, because the effort to exempt as much pollution control equipment as possible from tax and to encourage municipalities, private industry and so forth to continue with pollution control efforts has always been something in which I have been most interested. It is indeed unfortunate, but it is nevertheless a fact we have to face, that the bill before us provides no opportunity to move an amendment along the lines of the one that has been moved.
I have every sympathy in the world with the intent of the amendment to make certain municipal equipment tax free. However, in this case it is not the municipalities which are the manufacturers or producers. It is someone else. Accepting the amendment would not enable us to accomplish the intent which the hon. member desires. My hon. friend from Edmonton West has drawn attention to the difficulty in which we find ourselves. Although the amendment has been accepted by the Chair it would still, if approved, fail to produce any results along the lines we would like to see.
Taxation on equipment of this kind leads to some strange rulings. I would certainly like to see the position cleared up. Not many years ago, I was personally involved in a case concerning fairly large concrete tiles. The department ruled that if the tiles were to be installed horizontally and used for drainage they would be tax exempt, but if they were installed vertically and used for well tiles they would be subject to tax. While I wish we could accomplish what the hon. member has in mind, it does not seem possible to do so by way of this amendment, or even under this bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT

Mr. Chairman, while we are dealing with this clause of the bill, and dealing with provisions to improve the position of those who purchase materials to be used to control or eliminate pollution, I should like to refer to a parallel area of concern.
In addition to the direct attack upon pollution in which some municipalities and companies are engaged, an indirect approach is taking place. Many municipalities which have never done so before are now installing chlorinating facilities, using chlorine to make domestic water safe for use. In the past this has often not been considered necessary, but the growth of population and increasing concern about water purity has led to action on the part of a large number of smaller municipalities. While I realize it is probably not possible to take action at this point along the lines I have in mind, I suggest that when the next major review of the Excise Tax Act takes place the government should consider removing the tax from chlorine, an ingredient which is important to the maintenance of the health of the people. The municipalities most affected would be the smaller; municipalities, those which are least able to raise the taxes necessary to provide for programs of the kind I have mentioned. I believe the government
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
should encourage municipalities to take all possible measures for the good health of Canadians, and this is why I recommend strongly that the parliamentary secretary take note of the point I have made and use his best efforts to secure the removal of chlorine as a taxable item when the next revision of the act takes place, provided it is used for the chlorination of water within Canada.

speechtext:
There is no question that in this amendment my hon. friend from Moose Jaw is attempting to exempt municipalities from the incidence of excise tax in respect of anti-pollution equipment. It is also true he will not be able to accomplish everything he has set out to do in the amendment he has laid before the House. He is not able to do so because the government has not placed before us clauses whose amendment could effect that purpose. However, I think the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka gave in too soon.
In addition, it seems to me the parliamentary secretary was a bit out of line when he said the amendment would have the effect of making the clause nonsensical. Municipalities in Europe are going into the recycling of waste material in a big way and municipalities in North America will have to do the same if pollution is to be controlled. I should like to mention developments which are taking place on an experimental basis and which might well place municipalities in the position of becoming manufacturers. It is now possible to take celluloid products and turn them into protein. Municipalities could become involved in this process. It is now possible, on an experimental basis, to change human and animal waste into motive fuels. It may be necessary for municipalities to enter this processing field in an effort to beat their pollution problems.
The amendment before us would at least accomplish one thing. As the municipalities move into the recycling of waste, and turn out products which are useful in the marketplace, the costly facilities they will need for these purposes will be exempt from taxation. This will encourage municipalities to move into such areas of endeavour. As I say, municipalities in Europe have already done so. The amendment would make installations established by municipalities for these purposes exempt from taxation, and thus encourage municipalities to undertake endeavours of this kind.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know my hon. friend from Moose Jaw realized when drafting his amendment that there would be a real problem in arriving at a suitable wording. Since his amendment had to be kept in order he could not, of course, go beyond the wording of the bill.
The representations which have been made to the government and to all Members of Parliament by the Federation of Mayors and Reeves have been extensive and well thought out. We have all received press releases and briefs from the federation. So far, it seems, the government has chosen not to pay any attention to these representations. It is passing strange that ways can be found to exempt manufacturers and producers from excice tax with respect to equipment used for pollution control, but that similar action cannot be taken when municipalities are concerned. The minister, in his letter, said that providing

December 21, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
exemptions for municipalities would be a complicated matter, yet it is not complicated for the manufacturers and producers. That is a little hard not only for the mayors and reeves to swallow but for some of the members of the House to swallow as well.
Further, in his letter dated August 4, the Minister of Finance said that incinerators, though they may reduce waste, also cause air pollution and therefore he did not see how they could be exempted from the excise tax. Now, either the minister did not know or he conveniently forgot, but the president of the association, replying to the minister on August 16, pointed out that we now have the technology to manufacture incinerators that meet pollution control standards. He submitted they should, therefore, be exempt from excise tax. The minister makes a great deal about crushers not being exempt because they have no use other than facilitating the transportation of waste materials. If that argument is logical, then since pumping equipment, like crushers, are an integral part of a solid waste disposal system, why is pumping equipment exempt but not crushers?
These are some of the inconsistencies we see in this bill, some of which the hon. member attempts to solve in his amendment. If the wording of the amendment is not exactly as the parliamentary secretary would like it, he could get his officials or some of the roosters in the gallery to draft a proper amendment in the next minute or so. We are not particularly wedded to our wording. The mayors and reeves have pointed out that as a result of the bill the government's revenue from manufacturers and producers will be reduced by about $8 million a year. Why cannot the municipalities have an equivalent reduction in their costs?
If the amendment passes, no doubt it would cause some head scratching in the back rooms in terms of interpreting the regulations, but I am sure that problem can be solved. The municipalities have waited a long time for some relief in this area yet the Minister of Finance still finds excuses which I submit are unjustified. Although the parliamentary secretary might be hesitant to make any move that might displease the Minister of Finance, we do not feel the same way. Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to members on both sides of the committee supporting this amendment but at the same time admitting they have serious difficulty with the wording. I agree this is the case, particularly in view of the fact that under normal circumstances the manufacturing industry has not been primarily concerned with the disposal of waste. I am sure the parliamentary secretary would agree that unless manufacturing plants are provided with pollution control facilities we shall never be able to accomplish effective pollution control in this nation, particularly if we neglect one of the major sources of pollution in a given area, namely pollution resulting from municipal operations themselves. It used to be good enough for a municipality simply to burn its garbage and to dump its sewage into the nearest waterway. Although we are all aware that most industries used to dispose of their waste in this way, they now find it economically advantageous as well as environmentally advantageous to implement some form of pollution control.
It is true, as several of my colleagues have said, that municipalities will be subjected to pollution controls that are greatly different from any previous controls. All kinds of developments are taking place to produce useful byproducts from reclaimed waste, and many of these byproducts will come from fields with which we are not too familiar at the present time. Indeed, it may well be the case that a large segment of municipal workers will be engaged in producing byproducts from sewage and other forms of waste material. I bow to the superior wisdom of all members who were able to foresee many of the technical changes that are going to take place, such as the establishment in municipalities of pollution control methods that had not even been considered a few years ago. As most hon. members know, garbage has been reclaimed in some parts of California. From this reclamation hydrocarbon substances are derived which, when the process has been perfected, will be a valuable asset to the area and which they hope will heat much of the urban area that hitherto had been plagued by this very substance when it was in pollutant form.
It is quite possible, despite the remoteness of the subject today, that municipalities will be manufacturing, that there will be by-products and that the new technical changes involved will bring municipalities a great incentive to eliminate what has been possibly our major pollutant in the nation, municipal waste in all its various forms.
I am sure at this late stage in the session, and even at this late hour in the day, the parliamentary secretary will not recommend that this amendment go back to the officials for improvement. I say that not unkindly but because that is not the way the government operates. It would take a long time to think about that. I fail to see the minister being at all concerned with this amendment if it does not

I suggest there really is not much basis for objection to this amendment if we presuppose that municipalities will soon be in the manufacturing field. Municipalities will not be in this field in the same way industry is because the pollutants from industry must be recycled or handled some other way. I believe the government is now taking cognizance of this and is making concessions. The municipalities, however, will in fact be using pollutants as the primary source of their material for manufacture. I can see the day, and I suspect it will not be too remote, when the moneys which are being provided by this and other governments will be used to speed up our ability to develop programs and methods to dispose of municipal pollution in a much more efficient way. So I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that if he is right, and this amendment is not applicable to the municipalities today, there really should be no objection to passing it. If there are municipalities in the manufacturing field or which intend to manufacture, I presume from the wastes of the municipality, and in that way provide pollution control in a very important way which would improve the environment of the community, then what is wrong with that.
Although I cannot think of any municipality, and other members have not mentioned any specific municipality, that is in the production field, I suggest there are those of us, including you, Mr. Chairman, who believe this is inevitable because this government has basic environmental control legislation and is also working on the scientific developments that will make possible the improvement of the environment by the elimination of municipal pollution. Many municipalities across the country are still the biggest polluters of our lakes and rivers. The most important factor is not the amount of money that the government will have to expend, not the fact that every municipality will have to develop recycling machinery and manufacture something from the waste, but some technicality that the government has failed to take into consideration in drafting the bill. The vote on this amendment, which will take place shortly, will be an expression of opinion as to whether or not municipalities should be exempted from excise tax on recycling machinery. If the amendment carries this afternoon, I do not expect any earth shaking events to take place in the municipalities but I do believe that many of them will become more interested in creating a pollution free environment. That is what we as legislators should be concerned with. Every piece of legislation contains regulations which carry out the intent of the legislation. If the amendment is accepted, no doubt the regulations governing the application of the excise tax on recycling machinery could be drafted in such a way as to take into account the fact that the amendment is not in the right place.

Without a doubt he is one of the most knowledgeable members in the House with respect to the legal aspects of the legislation and the proper drafting of bills. His experience in the Chair has contributed a great deal to his knowledge and his insistence that the rules be followed is shown by his statement that this is not the right place for this amendment. It is regrettable that this matter was not considered more thoroughly when the bill was being drafted. However, all we can do at present as legislators is to express our intention that municipalities be encouraged to develop recycling machinery for waste products as quickly as possible. The old system of waste trenches and earth fills is no longer suitable. Very soon major cities will run out of available land and the old system cannot be used for many more years. Very often the chief advantage, after excise taxes are dropped, accrues to the people connected with a particular industry, to the manufacturers and others, and not to the consumer. I think, if we examine the facts, we shall see that this situation has come about over and over again. After all, this matter affects the people of Canada. It is because the taxpayers of Canada are being asked to pay higher taxes in certain fields, namely, higher personal income taxes and perhaps increased corporate taxes, that the government is able to remove the excise tax from certain areas.
This tax has contributed immensely to the national revenues. If taxpayers are being asked to pay increased personal income taxes in order to permit the lowering of certain prices to the consumer, I submit that we should make sure that the lower prices made possible by the elimination or reduction of excise taxes are passed on to the consumer. Until now there has been no evidence to indicate that this has been the case. It should not be necessary for a representative of the government to stand up and say, "Yes, we think this is a worthwhile suggestion and we shall consider it." After all, when tax reductions are not passed on, the government's own plans are frustrated. The government merely suggests that it is serving notice, through the reduction of excise taxes, that it wants price reductions passed on to the consumer. After that the whole thing sort of peters out, and nothing comes of it. I have yet to hear of any minister coming to the House and saying, "I have conducted a thorough investigation in this field and am satisfied that the amount of excise tax which has been taken off a product has been passed on to the consumer." These savings simply get lost in the shuffle.
I would think that a government that was interested in the consumer, and was interested in seeing that the taxes that were foregone resulted in lower prices, would be very pleased to have one of its representatives rise in the House

Mr. Speaker, we have listened to a good deal of discussion on aspects of municipal participation in the field of pollution control. The concessions which have been made to industry have been considered by the committee and by the House, and have been praised as being worthwhile. Hon. members have argued that similar consideration should be extended to that other major partner in the pollution field, the municipalities.
The municipalities have asked for concessions in connection with sales tax not only with respect to antipollution equipment but with respect to the materials used for municipal development generally. It is evident that the interests of the municipalities in controlling pollution and protecting the environment coincide with those of the provincial and federal governments, not to speak of the interests of the public as a whole. It has been our opinion that municipalities should be given full relief in respect to all pollution control activities in which they participate. It is true that sales tax is already being waived with respect to the purchase of certain types of equipment. Nevertheless, the municipalities are now entering into other fields, and if they are to succeed, their activities need the same favourable climate as the government is now offering to manufacturers.
In the course of the debate today several hon. members sought to show that industry was in a more favourable taxation position than were the municipalities, that the municipalities were really operating under a system of double taxation; an individual was obliged to pay tax to a municipality which, in turn, had to pay sales tax to the federal government in connection with goods used by the municipality and by the school board.
It may well be that in opening up the subject of sales tax generally, we in this party were handicapped by decisions reached by civil servants to the effect that only certain concessions could be made available at this time. Nevertheless, I submit that the arguments put forward today by a number of hon. members, prompted by representations made by those in the municipal field, are worthy of serious consideration.
On the government side, there appears to be an unwillingness to face the consequences of certain changes which are taking place. Consider, for example, the position of school boards which have amalgamated in order, among other things, to save expense on purchasing and maintenance. The limit of $3,000 on the exemption available to a very small school would certainly not be adequate to reflect the scale of operations of a much larger amalgamated school board. I point out that these particular operations do not interfere with any local industry or prejudice the jobs of local workmen. They are engaged in only to simplify the operation of supply and maintenance. All these arguments have been legitimately put forward, and they are deserving of consideration. If it were not for the Christmas spirit I would certainly consider moving that this question be referred back to the committee for further study. It is unlikely, though, that the parliamentary secretary would give any consideration to changing the legislation at this late date. After all, the bill before us goes back to July, 1971 and its provisions will apply fully in January, 1972. The"hon. member would probably argue, with some reason, that there is now no time left in which
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
to make major changes in the Excise Tax Act which would provide for concessions to be made to municipalities, school boards and other agencies.
I make a plea to the minister to consider in the near future making concessions to the municipalities which would enable them to engage fully in the work of pollution control. If there is anything in which young people today are interested collectively it is probably in some method of ending our destruction of the environment. Without a doubt we have gone through more resources in the last 20 years than the whole world had done in all the time which existed prior to that point. Young people today are identifying pollution as one of the major problems they have to face. Ten years ago our children were worried about the atomic bomb. They were saying there was no future for them because eventually the bomb would be dropped and we would all go up in smoke. Our young people do not feel this way today. They feel they have inherited a world that is badly polluted, an environment that has been destroyed. Our urban centres are not what our young people wish to have.
Much of the abuse of the environment stems from our inability to control pollution. Looking at the Ottawa River which flows past the Parliament Buildings we find water that is repulsive to drink. Indeed, it might be medically unsafe. Certainly, it has been medically unsafe at times to swim in it. It is true that some pollution comes from Renfrew and Pembroke which have industrial centres, and some comes from Timiskaming's pulp mill. Almost all of the pollution from the head of Lake Timiskaming, where I live, to the Ottawa River comes from human waste.
It seems to me we should make every concession possible to enable municipalities to purchase and instal pollution control equipment. We have an obligation to put the best brains in the National Research Council to work finding much better ways of handling sewage. In some other countries sewage has been turned into a very valuable commodity. With the technology available in the world today we could provide modern utilities to reclaim a great deal of value from sewage. We could return the water to the river almost pure enough to drink, and that would certainly eliminate pollution in the Ottawa River.
The reason the municipalities do not do this is money. What facilities there are are insufficient. We have put up money to construct lagoons, but in most areas these lagoons do not function properly. As most hon. members know, a lagoon is really a septic tank or pond into which you pump sewage. The water evaporates but eventually the pond fills up with solids and you have to construct another pond. In my particular area we have 37 inches of rain a year. If it were not for the thermal heat units in the area we would be hard pressed to evaporate 37 inches of water. About as much water is added to the lagoon in the form of precipitation as is extracted by evaporation. For six months out of the year the water freezes over, and obviously no evaporation takes place. If there is any runoff in the spring the pond overflows into the river, and the waste comes once again into the Ottawa River system.
The taxpayers have been paying a small fortune for these ponds and for the sewage systems that pipe the

effluent into the ponds. Yet I doubt that anyone has done any work on their feasibility for northern Ontario. The idea originated in the southern United States where I imagine about 200 inches of water evaporates every year. Although it is a good idea down there it is not so good when applied to northern Ontario. When people in northern Ontario ask their municipality for clean water, the water resources board of Ontario supplies a unit. I have attended the opening of several of these units, elaborate buildings, the grounds all nicely sodded, flags out front and so on. Water is taken out of some sewage laden lake, processed in the plant, and water sold to people on the street at a higher price than water from spring wells which have been used for 20 to 30 years.
My point is that we have not made sufficient effort to correct the situation. We still hear Members of Parliament saying that there should be a sales tax on that equipment.

When I began it was my intention to refer to the fact that the House, in its wisdom, decided in committee not to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) who is very interested in this subject of pollution and the problems the municipalities encounter every time they pay a tax to the government on something that is being made by one of their agencies. I think the government can make a contribution by removing the taxes the municipalities must pay, and I applaud the government today for allowing industry and manufacturers to be exempt from taxes in respect of pollution control equipment. subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this particular topic pursued by the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters), the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) and others has properly been very thoroughly examined. My intervention in this debate will not be lengthy. However, in saying that I must also put forward a point that there has been a great deal of debate all this fall on a number of topics much of which has been repetitive. I feel that, as a member, I am entitled to some time this afternoon to speak on behalf of the municipalities I represent in the Fraser Valley. The hon. member for Timiskam-ing mentioned the good work the municipal officers and
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
elected officials have done. He also mentioned the massive costs faced by the municipalities because of the extra services they are asked to provide which were not necessary when many municipalities were part of an agrarian society. Now, with greater technology and the movement to major cities the costs have intensified. The taxing power of the municipalities, however, has not kept pace.
In fact, I believe it is fair to say that the more dense the population of any municipality the higher the per capita cost faced by that municipality. I have some familiarity with this having at one time served on a municipal council. With the best will in the world, I think the members of that council were very conscious of the fact, living on the banks of the Fraser and concerned with environmental and sewage problems of that municipality and those surrounding, that they should do something about this problem of antipollution and pollution abatement. The point is, however, that we did not really accomplish this although we did establish a sewer system. Most of the sewage went to its destination in Burrard Inlet or the Fraser River without the benefit of even primary treatment.
So when we are talking about cleaning up our environment we are talking about costs facing cities and municipalities across the country. Of the nine municipalities that I represent in the Lower Fraser I do not know one that is not dumping raw sewage into either the Fraser or Burrard Inlet. We are a little hypocritical about this. When the government appoints, perhaps for appearances only, a new ministry called the ministry of the environment, that looks great. But we are not serious about this, because the government makes this appointment in the hope that perhaps we can clean up our environment and take steps to curtail its constant erosion caused by technology and increased population, and this looks great, but it is only a public relations job if we do not also assist, through taxation and other measures, the various levels of government which can take the steps necessary to clean up the environment.
Last night on CBC there was an excellent documentary at 10 p.m. to 10.30 p.m., I believe. It dealt with the interrelated problems of food chains, the population explosion and pollution. Anybody who watched that program knows that many people are concerned that, if we persist in the expansionist-minded preoccupation with the GNP, technology, crowding, population explosion and all the rest of it, we will prove that Malthus was right and that ultimately we are leading toward the destruction of human life on this planet.
I feel as strongly about the kind of thing we might be doing here to combat pollution as I do about the lunacy of the nuclear arms race, regardless of which country happens to be engaged in it at the moment. If we are really serious about attempting to make the world a more liveable place for perhaps another generation or two, then we most devote considerable funds to our fight against pollution. It makes no sense to me to be encouraging the municipalities, through the Department of the Environment, on the one hand to clean up their own backyards and on the other to deny them federal assistance through tax laws to do it. It is contradictory.

We have done the same thing with the Canada Water Act which, incidentally, was passed approximately two years ago. Not one river basin board has been developed in any province since then; but what is worse, we have done something similar to what we are doing here. We have set up the Canada Water Act and the particular agency to administer the act, without providing one cent of federal funds to assist in the cleaning up of the various river basins so as to achieve decent water standards across Canada. So we are not talking about piddling or insignificant things here. It is not just a matter of whether or not we should give a tax break on some sewer pipe to some municipality, which the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Whelan) says is tax free anyway, but we are attempting to reflect the whole concern of our party and the people we represent and, I am sure, members on all sides of the House, about where we are going environmentally.

Last evening, and again this afternoon, we asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to give serious consideration to the representation of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities all across Canada. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have not previously advised the Clerk that consultations have resulted in a desire to deal now with Bill S-9, the Copyright Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill S-9, an Act to amend the Copyright Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
That Bill S-9, an Act to amend the Copyright Act, be amended by deleting from Clause 1 lines 15 to 23 inclusive and substituting therefor:
"(4) "Copyright" in respect of the contrivances mentioned in the preceding sub-section shall have the meaning ascribed to it by sub-section (1) of section 3 of this Act with the exception of the sole rights to perform the contrivance or any substantial part thereof in public or to communicate the contrivance by radio communication."

He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment is a technical one, not substantive. Its purpose is to assure that following the passage of Bill S-9 record producers will be left with the right to protect themselves against record piracy and/or unlawful reproduction and distribution of their products.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) stated in the committee that he wants to protect record producers against this type of piracy, that he wants them to retain all their other rights under copyright except performing rights. There is no disagreement between the minister and myself on substance but we do disagree on the wording of the bill.
After repeated examination of the bill I am convinced that the words in it do not protect the record producers against piracy. The minister and his advisers say that the words in the bill do protect them. Our disagreement is on legal drafting and it is an important disagreement. It is important because if the bill is passed in its present form it will not only take away the record producers' performing rights but also many of the other rights that protect them against record piracy. I shall explain this in greater detail.
Under the Copyright Act, section 4(3), record producers are given the protection of copyright. In order to determine the meaning of copyright for record producers under that section We have to look at the definition section, which is section 3(1). Under that section we find that copyright comprises a package of four more basic
Copyright Act
rights-the right to produce, the right to reproduce, the right to perform, and the right to publish. This means that no one but the holder of the copyright can produce the work, reproduce the work, perform the work, or publish the work unless the holder of the copyright grants a licence to another person to do these things, or unless royalties are paid to the holder.
These are the rights which a record producer presently holds under the Copyright Act. Now the minister has decided that it is not proper for record producers to have performing rights under the Copyright Act and he introduces this bill to take away that right. But what does he do? Instead of leaving the record producers all their copyright rights under section 3(1) except performing rights, he takes away all their rights under that section in section 1(4) of Bill S-9 a new definition of copyright for records. The definition says that for records copyright will mean the sole right to reproduce.
In other words, if Bill S-9 passes, the only right under copyright retained for record producers will be the right to reproduce. Whereas the record producers had four basic rights under the Copyright Act, under Bill S-9 they will have only one basic right, the right to reproduce, and this despite the fact that the government said it wanted to take away only one right. If we are interested in taking away only one right, the performing right, they should be left with three rights, the right to produce, the right to reproduce, and the right to publish. Why is the government leaving them with only one right? I can say that by taking away the production and publishing rights in addition to the performing right, Bill S-9 seriously handicaps the record producers in protecting themselves against record piracy.
This handicap is confirmed by the provisions in the recent treaty against record piracy which was concluded in Geneva on October 29, 1971. This treaty was signed by Canada. Section 2 of the treaty provides that each signatory state shall protect the record producer against reproduction and importation for distribution. After the passage of Bill S-9 Canadian record producers will have protection against reproduction but not against importation for redistribution. One wonders how the Canadian government can sign a treaty saying one thing and then introduce a bill saying another thing.
Furthermore, in attempting to accomplish the same goal the United States Congress passed a bill, U.S.646, on November 15, 1971, providing protection against reproduction and distribution. Bill S-9 provides protection only against reproduction. To correct this defect in Bill S-9 I have introduced the amendment before the House which would leave the record producers all the rights they presently possess under section 3(1) of the Copyright Act except performing rights and radio broadcasting rights. I have included broadcasting rights because the broadcasting companies are most concerned. My amendment reads:
That Bill S-9, an act to amend the Copyright Act, be amended by deleting from clause 1 lines 15 to 23 inclusive and substituting therefor:

December 21, 1971
Copyright Act
(4) "Copyright" in respect of the contrivances mentioned in the preceding subsection shall have the meaning ascribed to it by subsection (1) of section 3 of this act with the exception of the sole rights to perform the contrivance or any substantial part thereof in public or to communicate the contrivance by radio communication.
I say, let us leave the record producers all the rights they presently have except the right to perform and broadcast. In conclusion, I repeat that my amendment does nothing to change the principal purpose of this bill. It does, however, attempt to protect record producers in Canada against piracy of their works which the minister himself said he wishes to protect. I hope the government and the House will see fit to pass this amendment and grant justice to the record producers of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. R. Tolmie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill S-9 before the House was introduced in Parliament over a year ago. Because it is extremely short one would think it would be extremely simple. However, this is not the case and a great deal of parliamentary time and consideration has been given to this conceptually difficult legislation before appearing here for third reading. I want to thank members on all sides of the House for their willingness to deal with this legislation and for the help they provided in committee.
This is a most difficult area of law, perhaps because it deals with rights in respect of intellectual property. At the present time authors and composers of music have, and exercise, the right to extract money from radio and television stations and a whole host of other organizations that use music commercially, as payment for the use of their intellectual works. In 1967, the eight very large, foreign-owned record companies that produce 90 per cent of the records sold in Canada each year claimed the same right. They asked for a fee that would have had the effect of extracting about $4 million per year from the Canadian broadcasting industry.
The government had serious misgivings about this application, for three reasons. First, it was felt that this was wrong in principle, that while authors and composers have no other way of receiving fair remuneration for their work except fees for their public performance, the record industry does very well from the sale of records. Second, the government had referred the whole question of intellectual and industrial property to the Economic Council for review in 1966 and it was reluctant to see a new performing right exercised in the interim. Third, it was felt that the Canadian broadcasting industry, which bears great responsibility for the achievement of national goals in Canada as a matter of public policy, should not be required also to bear these extra costs-needless and unfair extra costs, in my view.
SRL withdrew their 1969 and 1970 tariff of fees but went ahead late last year with a tariff for 1971. The government met this with Bill S-9. Subsequently, the Economic Council reported and recommended the abolition of a performing right in records. Bill S-9 was considered at length by committees of both the Senate and the House of Commons. Every interest has been heard with regard to this legislation and, I might add, heard at length. I am opposed to the amendment which has been proposed.
[Mr. Allmand.l
It was suggested at the last minute that Bill S-9 removed more rights than it purported to do and affected more than merely the performing right in records. This was a matter of great concern, and to be absolutely certain that these allegations were without foundation the officials of the department were instructed to meet with representatives of those opposing the passage of the bill to consider the legal argument they were putting forward. As well, the advice of the Department of Justice was requested. I should add that we have several of the country's leading specialists in this field employed as consultants to the department. They were unanimous in their unequivocal endorsation of Bill S-9 as it presently stands. Furthermore, this position was fully supported by the considered opinion of the law officers of the Department of Justice.
I want to assure the House that Bill S-9 is designed solely to remove the alleged performing right in sound recordings and that the wording used does precisely what it purports to do, and nothing more. Allegations that this legislation, when enacted, would promote infringement of sound recordings have no substance in fact.
Two other points were raised in the Justice Committee and I would like to allude to them. First is the concern expressed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) regarding the inequitable position of performers. The Copyright Act is now being revised, and I think the minister expressed his concern and his sympathy for the position of the performers and stated quite unequivocally that the point made by Mr. Dodge of the CLC and by the hon. member will be kept in mind during the revision of the act.
This legislation is effective from January 1 this year, and some have argued that this has the taint of retroactivity. I dispute this because the record manufacturers have at all times known, and have been on notice, that the government would not stand idly by should they press their case for a tariff before the Copyright Act revision was before this House. When they did so last year, the government introduced this legislation and the parties affected were clearly aware of the fact that any performing right they had would be removed, effective January 1.
As an example of what might be considered retroactive legislation, a budget speech may not be followed by legislation for several months yet it is from the date of the budget speech that the legislation is made effective. This legislation is no different. Parliament has the power to specify when an act shall come into force, and while the legislation can have no effect until passed, public notice of the date intended for commencement was given so that persons could adjust their affairs if they wished.
Mr. Speaker, this bill received a detailed hearing in the Senate and was considered at length by a committee of this House. Its full implications were considered by the Deputy Minister of Justice and by his officers, as well as by the department's officials and consultants. I commend this legislation to the House.
