speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
Order. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock tonight.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
December 21, 1971
The House resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues in the official opposition have agreed that there shall be one speaker only on Bill S-9. It seems most convenient to make that speech at the report stage, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) having pretty well put the issue before us with his amendment. I hope that I will be allowed to make the whole speech and then have it done with.
I think it will please all members of the House when I say that Canadian talent does reap its own reward and that last year, and I am speaking of the full calendar year, over $5.5 million was paid by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and various stations which make up the Canadian Association of Broadcasters to the artists, performers and composers of Canada. That is how much the Canadian broadcasting industry paid to these people. Clearly, artistic merit in this country is recognized substantially.
The issue that we are concerned about does not involve directly, although it might indirectly, the authors, composers and publishers as such. What it does involve is whether performing rights such as I have mentioned should be extended to the broadcasting or other public performance of recordings. It is this issue which brings Bill S-9 before the House. Is the right to broadcast or play recordings in public a proper right?
It has been argued, Sir, that if I am an automobile dealer and I decide to sell you an automobile and somebody else an automobile for the same price, I cannot, if the other purchaser decides to use that automobile in the taxi business, say to him, "Since you will make extra money out of this automobile which you are to use for commercial purposes I can, therefore, charge you extra for it." That, substantially, is the position the recording companies are asking us to adopt when they ask us to defeat Bill S-9. I say, on my own behalf and on behalf of my associates, that we reject that position of the recording companies. I want that clear on the record. We reject that position and therefore we are fundamentally in agreement with the principles set forth in Bill S-9. Let there be no mistake about that.
Hear, hear!

Later in my speech, which will be remarkably brief, I will point out what I think was the error in the presentation of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. Nevertheless, we owe him a debt since at least he has put the issue before us and has presented in the best possible way one side of the argument. It does not appear that many support this position.
We find ourselves in distinguished company in rejecting the position of the recording industry and its friends. One could go back to someone with whom older parliamentarians in this House served, namely, J. L. Ilsley, one time member for Annapolis-Kings, and subsequently Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. In 1957 he brought in a far reaching report on copyright. He headed a royal commission on copyright. The Ilsley commission,
Copyright Act
in dealing with an issue similar to the one before us tonight recommended in part:
The act restricted by the copyright in a sound recording should be the making of a record embodying the record.
In other words, as suggested earlier by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Tolmie), the only right that should be protected is the right to reproduce. I think that is an important argument because, as the mover of the amendment has suggested and as the spate of telegrams which has arrived in the last couple of days has suggested, the piracy that takes place in the reproduction of records can be cured if we reject the principle of Bill S-9. I hope I can show in my speech that this argument is utterly fallacious. In any event, those who agree with Bill S-9 find themselves in good company, not only with the Ilsley Royal Commission on Copyright but with the report of the Economic Council of Canada. I quote a portion of that report which deals with this matter:
We continue to accept the concept of a performing right in the basic material because this is the only way in which a writer of such materials can get payment related to the use of his work in the market. The record maker on the other hand, in spite of many creative inputs by his staff, is really in the business of selling a physical item such as a disc or tape and it is this activity that should reimburse him.
I think that puts the point very well. I mentioned telegrams. I think it should go on record that counsel for the main opponent of this bill, in a last effort to hold off passage of Bill S-9, telephoned the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). I quote from his telegram:
-it was prepared not to exercise any of the rights which it presently enjoys under the Canadian Copyright Act pending a complete revision of the said act.
This is their latest position. It is an attempt to hold off passage of Bill S-9. I understand the minister is ill and cannot be here. I take it from the fact the measure was called and we are now debating it that the government has in fact rejected this last-ditch effort of the opponents of the bill. The parliamentary secretary indicates that this is precisely the position.
It does not disturb me very much that such an attempt was turned down. I think we are proceeding on the right course of principle. In my opinion, there is no reason to accept such a request. I do not think the right should have existed in the first place, if in fact it does exist under the present law. I am not prepared to concede that. The issue was never determined in the courts. I think we are bound on the right course. My conscience will not give me a twinge because I support the passage of Bill S-9.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary will take this message to his minister. We have been told over and over again in various committees, particularly the broadcasting committee, when dealing with performing rights and the creative abilities of Canadian artists, that there is desperate need for a new Copyright Act in Canada. The Economic Council of Canada has released its recent study. I hope we can expect some action in regard to the Copyright Act.

December 21, 1971
Copyright Act
I think in a moment or two I will be able to point out that the piracy argument, while a fallacious one with regard to the principle we are studying this evening still deserves some kind of answer. In the Globe and Mail, the second last page of the entertainment section, there is an article from Hollywood about the millions of dollars lost to record pirates. This points out the problem in the American recording industry. One witness who appeared before the justice committee said that as much as 25 per cent of the material sold as records in Canada represented pirate material. These were tapes brought across the American border. Believe it or not, most of our taping is done in the United States. As much as 25 per cent of the Canadian record industry can be said to be based on pirate operations. There is need for enforcement in that field.
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace spoke about piratical operations. There is a provision in the Copyright Act to deal with that. It is a question of better enforcement. During the discussion in committee, the Commissioner of Patents, Mr. A. M. Laidlaw, was faced with this argument about pirates. He said, as recorded at page 51 of issue No. 43 of the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs:
-that right is derived from the fact that the manufacturer gets the right to produce either from the composer by the assignment of that right, or secondly through compulsory licensing provisions which are set out in section 19 of the act.
The hon. member can look there for the remedies that the recording industry now have and enjoy. The point about piracy was made by myself in an exchange with Mr. Laidlaw. I quote from the following page:

Could I boil it down? It seems to me that the one fact we are faced with here is no matter what SRL has as its interpretation of the law there is no change made whatsoever by what we are being asked to pass. Am I correct in saying no change whatsoever? If they were in trouble before, they will be in trouble in the future, but that is up to a better revision of copyright law. Am I correct in stating it that way?
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
And better enforcement.
That is the problem. It is not to put something new in the law, as suggested by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, but to put bigger teeth in the law, have a better method of enforcement or a higher penalty so that it is worth while tracking down the people who engage in pirate operations. I suspect that what is happening in Canada, with the remarkable amount of high-priced talent engaged on both sides of the issue and some considerable lobbying on both sides, is some sort of trial run for events in much larger markets such as the United States, West Germany and the United Kingdom. I am suspicious when I see counsel, who normally earn $1,000 an hour on enterprises like this, standing around. I do not think they are here for the amount of money that can be gained, even if the recording industry in Canada is successful against the broadcasting industry. The chips on the table are of such a size that we can imagine there is a far greater gain involved.
There is a provision in the bill that would make this law retroactive to January 1, 1971. If the recording industry had a right which it tried to exercise this year, that right would be wiped out by the retroactive provision that we have in this law. My colleagues and I resisted that in the

committee. If the House were proceeding at a different time of year I would found my doubts in a motion to strike out that part of the law. However, we are getting near the end of the session and Parliament can only do so much.
I talked this matter over with the recording industry. They are not so concerned about the difference a year will make as they are with winning the whole ball game. They are not going to win the whole ball game, so I do not feel too badly about not putting the issue to the House. The issue of retroactivity was well scouted in the Justice committee. My colleagues and I put forth the best arguments we could. When the matter was put to a vote after several hours, we stood alone; we could not persuade others of the righteousness of our cause.
I know my colleagues would want me to say, in the one speech to be made on this bill on behalf of my party, that in this regard the principle is the same: we are unalterably opposed to the imposition of retroactive provisions which could take a possible existing right and remove it by act of Parliament. We generally approve the principle of the bill and accordingly wish it to become the law of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity to say a few words concerning Bill S-9, entitled an Act to amend the Copyright Act. I leafed through the proceedings of the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, which devoted several meetings to consideration of the bill to amend the Copyright Act, and I was very much impressed by the convincing evidence given to that committee by some organizations and individuals.
I also received many representations from people directly or indirectly affected by Bill S-9, and I came to the conclusion that we should support the bill under study.
The bill is simple, I think. It concerns the removal from the act of the performing rights of record manufacturers or other owners of sound reproduction equipment, as if the record or perforated roll was in itself a musical or artistic work.
Evidence was produced before the Senate committee to the effect that if radio broadcasters, for example, had to pay fees as demanded by the consortium of large record companies, it would cost record producers over $4.5 million a year, of which more than $800,000 would be paid by the CBC alone.
Sound Recording Licences, which groups MCA, RCA, Warner Bros., London, Columbia, Polydor, Capitol and others-all American companies with the exception of two that are German or British-is asking for 2.6 per cent of the gross income of private radio stations, 0.5 per cent from private television stations and 4 cents per capita from the CBC, and that adds up to additional payments of over $4 million.
I must admit that over 75 per cent of that amount would leave the country because those companies are foreign-based and have only branches in Canada and the recordings are only reproductions of the initial recording.
December 21, 1971

It is true that in Great Britain record manufacturers are protected under the Copyright Act but such is not the case in the United States. Should Canada reject the amending measures under discussion, the majority of record companies which are only branches of American companies from which they obtain the original recordings would benefit in Canada of a right which the American government denies them. We are not as rich as the Americans and we should therefore act accordingly.
In his testimony before the Senate committee, the President of the Baton Broadcasting Ltd., of Ontario, Mr. Goodman, has proved that 90 per cent of all 11-inch records sold in Canada are subject to a per unit royalty of 60 cents that is paid over to the parent company which has delivered the licence to its Canadian branch plant.
Another aspect to be considered is that Bill S-9 does not purport to limit in any way the rights of artists, otherwise I would be one of the first to rise against such a restriction because we have in Canada very talented artists who deserve to be encouraged and whom the government should assist financially to enable them to improve their ability to the benefit of Canada as a whole.
We should emphasize, first of all the testimony of the right hon. J. L. Isley as contained in a brief he submitted in 1957 to the Royal Commission of inquiry on copyright and I quote the following from page 77:
The act restricted by the copyright in a sound recording should be the making of a record embodying the recording.
At the present time it would appear that an unauthorized public performance of a recording embodied in a record is an infringement of the copyright in the record. . , . We recommend the abolition of a record manufacturer's performing right and broadcasting right in records or in the recording embodied in the record.
In its Report on Intellectual and Industrial Property the Economic Council stated in January 1971:
It is presently stated in the Copyright Act that a particular sound recording as such has a 50-year protection against direct copying, just as does a photograph. A major point at issue here is the associated performing right in such a recording whereby a record-maker would have, like the writer of the words and music, a legal claim to collect a fee from public users of his product above and beyond the original sale price of the recording.
I still recognize the principle of the right of performance or of representation concerning the original work since that is the only way the author can obtain remuneration for the use of his work on the market.
However, as concerns the recording producer, even if his staff does valuable and truly creative work, his trade is the sale of a purely material thing, that is a record or a magnetic tape, and he must expect his remuneration from that trade. To say that he also deserves a royalty each time his product is used publicly would mean that the publisher of a book is entitled to a supplement each time the book is read.
This is why I support Bill S-9 now before the House. I consider that the artists whose works are broadcast day in and day out over the radio and in all parts of Canada are enjoying a free and extraordinary publicity which deserves to be recognized by the artists themselves, and I do not see why these same artists would oppose the passing of Bill S-9 which, in a way, protects them against those who sometimes exploit them very dishonestly.
Copyright Act
I for one consider that Bill S-9, besides protecting the Canadian radio stations, at the same time provides the Canadian artists with a protection that they did not enjoy before. In fact, they will no longer be exploited by American firms, to the prejudice of the artists and the Canadian people in general.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to give my support to Bill S-9 in the course of this debate because I deem it fair and useful not only to the artists but also to the Canadian radio stations.

Mr. Speaker, we are considering an amendment put forward by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand). Since it was agreed that we would have one spokesman from each party and limit debate on the bill, perhaps I might be permitted to speak briefly to the amendment and later to the main motion.
I should like first of all to say that I am not particularly impressed with the piracy argument that is asserted in telegrams I have been receiving. It seems to me there was considerable discussion of these matters in the committee and that this question was resolved, certainly to my satisfaction if not to the satisfaction of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. He is a lawyer, and if he took the trouble to read section 4 that is being amended it seems to me very little more protection could be offered recording companies than that already provided.
This afternoon the hon. member suggested that the right of reproduction is protected here, though he had some doubt about the right of dissemination-at least, if I understood him correctly. It seems to me that if you control the right of reproduction you also control the right of dissemination because, after all, it is very difficult to disseminate something that has not been reproduced. I do not usually associate the statements of the minister with competence, though of course we always have competent statements from his parliamentary secretary. I can see no reason why any government in its right mind-and from time to time we do ask that question about this government-would put itself in the position of supporting any measure that would invite piracy in this country of intellectual and artistic properties. That argument just does not wash with me.
Have you really anything to worry about?

I do not know that I have, because I have no intellectual or artistic properties to protect at the moment. But I should like to say that I think this whole thing is a red herring, and although I have a great personal regard for the hon. member I regret that I cannot support his amendment. Perhaps enough has been said about that for the moment.
My views about this legislation are well known to anyone who cares to read the minutes of proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which considered this bill for five, six sessions or more. Therefore I shall not go into the legal history of Sound Recording Licences' attempt, after over a quarter of a century's silence, to assert some right under the Copyright Act to levy a performance fee on radio stations in addition

December 21, 1971
Copyright Act
to that already paid by radio stations to performing rights societies such as CAPAC and BMI.
As I have said, I shall not go into the history of the matter for those who know the issues involved. Those who do not, probably do not care anyway. However, I must say at the outset that I speak on behalf of my party in direct support of Bill S-9. I regard the move by SRL, a foreign-dominated collection of huge recording companies, as little more than another grab at the public's pocket book. I feel that anyone examining the history of this industry would come to the conclusion that the ethics of this particular group are far from savoury.
SRL has fought a hard fight. It was a battle complete with high-priced legal help and a flurry of telegrams to MPs. Although I hate to say this, I think there has also been a manipulation of performers, and included in this manipulation were the struggling Canadian recording companies. And all this in an effort to support their claim. It seems to me that the local, indigenous recording companies and performers were perhaps forced to accept the benevolence of SRL only because they really had no other alternative. The blame for that, I think, we can lay directly at the door of government-perhaps not this government but historically at Canadian governments. I want to speak about that later.
I think we should examine what is behind this big push by SRL to assert there was some previously existing right under the Copyright Act. Two years ago SRL suddenly decided it wanted to assert this right and to go before the copyright appeal board with their case. Why were the stakes regarded as so high that it warranted such an expensive campaign? I think it is worth thinking about that question. If SRL's performance fee were legitimized in Canada, a foot in the door would be established for making an onslaught on the lucrative and huge market in the United States. It was important to establish that foothold here in line with the pattern of precedence.
Before the committee, SRL claimed that it knew this performance fee was paid in Europe and perhaps in Australia; therefore, logically it should be paid in Canada. If they go to the United States legislators and say this has happened in Europe, in Australia and now in Canada, how can you contradict the logic that it should apply in the United States? Conditions are not at all congruous. There are many state-owned radio stations. As a matter of fact, the situation in Europe does not at all prevail in Canada. I think that is the loophole in their argument.
Nevertheless, the SLR is playing for stakes much larger than their always-amended-downward claims. Of course they want, and need to get, and right now, into the United States market. That is why they are here. That is why they were willing to ask for assistance from various people such as performers and perhaps indigenous record manufacturers. I do not think any of us can buy that argument. The United States Congress, for example, for years has repudiated similar initiatives as those put forward by SRL. That is part of the history.
I think at this point it is important for me to say that while I completely reject the concept of performance rights as a charge on Canadian radio stations by recording companies, radio stations are currently paying fees to
(Mr. Rose.]
certain performing rights societies such as BMI which is owned by United States radio stations, and also CAPAC which is the equivalent of ASCAP in the United States, to the extent of 2.6 per cent of a station's gross revenue. The stations pay that whether they are music stations or top show stations.
I reject the idea of additional performance rights being granted these particular companies, for a variety of reasons. I shall not necessarily reveal these tonight. Certainly we examined a number of these reasons in the committee. I do not believe certain radio stations are paying too much for their principal product. They have music and I do not believe they are paying too much for this. The music they play is their reason for existence in most cases. I do not think their fees to BMI or CAPAC are unnecessarily burdensome. The fees the stations pay to BMI and CAPAC ultimately fall back to the truly creative individuals in the complex chain which ultimately results in the record. The fees paid by the radio stations through CAPAC and BMI go back to the creative people, the publishers and the composers.
A colleague asked me if I would give an illustration of what is BMI and CAPAC. I thought I had said earlier that BMI is a performing rights society owned by American radio stations and that its full name is Broadcast Music Institution. CAPAC is the Canadian Association of Publishers and Composers. In saying these things it should be recognized that the manufacturer of a $6 disc or record, such as Columbia or Capitol, is not rewarded directly by the radio station, but the publisher and composer receive approximately 2 cents each time the record is played. Publishers and composers are not amply rewarded for their creative efforts. I think the main plot of this enterprise, which is described by the council for SLR as a troika, is for the record companies to get more than the people who probably came up with the intellectual property in the first place.
The real "kicker" is that before most songs are released by most major companies represented by SRL, the company insists on obtaining the publishing rights from the composer and thus along with benefiting from the sale of the record for $6 the recording company also gets the publishing rights and therefore receives the one cent from BMI and CAPAC. In addition, I believe it is well recognized that the eight major recording companies represented by SRL are among the most vertically and horizontally integrated companies in the world. They own publishing companies, sheet music companies, broadcasting stations and a network. They control the industry down to the retail level. They can make or break a particular performer. They are interested in areas far removed from the music business. They are exceptionally greedy. They want to grab as much as they can possibly grab from any particular segment of society.
SRL's attempt to defeat Bill S-9 makes me sick. This is the reason, in spite of the fact that I have certain reservations, I shall vote with the government and support, of all people, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, which also gives me some feelings of discomfort from time to time because while the Canadian Association of Broadcasters was very agile in supporting the government's position as against SRL's performing rights I am quite certain that if certain performing individuals such as
December^!, 1971

actors or singers attempted to establish a performing rights society here in Canada to reward the performers for their particular residual right, there would be almost a revolt or at least a reaction from these same people. CAB is for performers so long as SRL is going to get the action, but I wonder what their reaction would be if the performers approached the radio stations with their own performance group.
I should like to spend a minute or two on my real concern. While I do not, as I have said, support SRL's performance rights, in the words of at least two very famous men I want to make perfectly clear that I do support performing rights as opposed to performance rights. These performance rights have been asserted by various creative people through AFM ACTRA and Actors Equity, who have expressed support for the rejection of Bill S-9. I am also in sympathy with the struggles of our indigenous recording industry. I am not talking about the subsidiaries, but about the idigenous recording industry about which I am sure my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) spoke a moment ago.
I would like to see this indigenous industry flourish as a positive cultural force in our country. I think we should do all we can to assist them in developing the Canadian culture. We spend millions of dollars doing this in other areas. The creative people, through the CLC, appeared before the committee and took a position against the passage of Bill S-9 chiefly because SRL was the only group which recognized the residual rights of performers to benefit from any ongoing success of their intellectual properties.
I think it might be well to briefly underline what happens. If you happen to be the composer of a very successful work that is recorded you can receive benefit through CAPAC copyright for up to 50 years perhaps. If you are a fiddle player on an Anne Murray record you play your recording date; according to the contract it might end up as a $90 session, and from there on you are out in the cold. It seems logical to me that if one participates positively in creating a very successful recording as a performer in the backbenches of a musical group, that performer has a right, because of his efforts to be part of the success of that recording, along with the publisher and the composer. So I support performing rights as opposed to performers' rights as applied to recording companies, especially those which are not Canadian owned.
Why were the performing groups such as ACTRA, the Musicians Union and Actors Equity opposed to Bill S-9? They were opposed because they had years of frustration in dealing with the government in an attempt to have their residual rights recognized as a basic right in our copyright law. As a result of their frustration they used SRL as a vehicle to advance and publicize these claims which have been ignored by the government for years. SRL was merely a court of last resort for the performers and creative people. It is regrettable that this is so. It seems to me that Canadian recording companies and Canadian performers are getting into bed with SRL as the elephant, but all they will get out of it is a peanut. So I do not support their claim, and I regret to have to say this.
Copyright Act
The parliamentary secretary, kind, honourable and handsome gentleman that he is, said this afternoon that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) is sympathetic to the economic aspirations of Canadian performers. What good is sympathy? One thing the government has been able to do for these people for years, perhaps above all else, is to give sympathy. That is hardly enough at this point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but I must do so to remind him that the time allotted to him has expired. The hon. member may continue if there is unanimous consent. Is there such consent?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Say something.
I thank kind hon. members in all quarters of the House for allowing me perhaps one or two minutes to say something in conclusion. So I will proceed with the climax of this speech-
Hear, hear!

-as expeditiously as possible, and I promise in gratitude that I will not insist on the performing right. I believe it is recognized by the government that we need a complete overhaul of the Copyright Act. I think we need also-in fact, I am very determined about it-to push for a kind of amendment which would result in establishing in Canada once and for all the residual rights of Canadian performers to participate in the ongoing benefits of an artistic property in which they participated. That is crucial. When the copyright was first developed we dealt mainly with the print medium. That was not really airtight. But technological changes since that time have forced us to take a new look at the whole area of artistic and intellectual properties. I am pleased that the government is looking into this matter and I wish them success.
I have a suggestion to make. Let us boost the total charge on radio stations from 2.6 per cent to about 3 per cent. Let us distribute to CAPAC and BMI a grand total of about 2 per cent of the station's gross, which would ultimately flow to publishers and composers. Let us take the 1 per cent, or as it would work out according to the CRTC one-third Canadian content regulation, and through some kind of Canadian performance society distribute that one-third of the gross to Canadian performers and record companies through some formula. I am not hung-up on the particular figures; it is the proportion and the recognition of the rights that concern me. But why not try to develop such an amended formula? Who can quarrel with it?
I do not think stations would quarrel with it if the total required for performance fees with performance rights associations came down slightly or went up slightly. I do not think they can quarrel basically and philosophically with this suggestion. Certainly the Canadian performers would not quarrel with it. They would probably be very pleased because through SRL they would be making an effort to establish what they consider to be a very basic and crucial right for their own economic and cultural

December 21, 1971
Copyright Act
benefit, and that is why I am supporting this bill. Who in Canada needs SRL anyway?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that most of us have received representations from radio stations and other broadcasting outlets concerning this bill. I support the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) this evening and I am pleased that the amendment was turned down.
We have always wanted sufficient funds provided for Canadian performers in order to encourage them to stay in Canada rather than going to the United States for higher wages. We were pleased with the recent decision made by the CBC to retain a particular performer on a salary basis, as a result of which he will remain in Canada and develop his talents here. We have a very favourable record in the development of Canadian talent. One has only to watch American TV shows to see the influence that Canadians have on them. I found it interesting the other night listening to Mr. Olson doing what I did not realize at the beginning was a spoof on the influence of Canadian artists on American culture. He named individuals and stressed the number of Canadians who are participating in American programming. Most of them got their start on Canadian TV but went south of the border because they could earn more money there. It was a very good program.
I believe we have an influence on American cultural affairs far out of proportion to our size. Any effort made to provide greater reward to artists in Canada, to enable them to stay here, is worth while. Therefore, it was with some trepidation that I learned an agency had been formed in Canada to collect certain fees, not to give money to performers participating in the arts here but on behalf of the companies manufacturing records. These companies, under this arrangement, were going to get a rake off every time a record was played on a disc jockey show. Canadian talent is not second rate, but perhaps it suffers from the same fate as that of the prophet who is spurned in his own land. We did not really appreciate Wayne and Shuster half as much when they were doing weekly shows in Canada as we do now when they come to us via an American network with their own special shows.

The CRTC regulation requiring greater use of Canadian talent has been beneficial. I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West that funds be increased for the purpose of providing artists and performers with a major share of the revenue. If we are going to allow radio stations to be charged a fee every time they play a record, and the revenue is to go to the companies which press records, we may well see some radio stations playing old records on which the copyright has run out after expiration of the seven-year limitation. I agree that the government has taken a proper step in this case to correct what many radio stations consider to be an abuse by record companies which are united with other companies in an agency set up for their self-help rather than for the sake of helping performers, artists, directors and others connected with the industry.
An important factor to remember is that disc jockeys play a large role in the merchandising of new Canadian talent. Records are donated to them by the record companies. The royalty that a performer receives depends on the volume of sales of his record beyond a certain figure. If a disc jockey likes a certain record, plays it repeatedly and it becomes a hit and is bought in the record stores, then the artist and the orchestra which provided the background benefit. Any curtailment on the use of such records will make it more difficult for newcomers to get into the field. I am told that about only one out of every thousand records becomes a hit. Most of the records played by disc jockeys do not find ready acceptance. Disc jockeys play a major role in communities which are served by only one local radio station. In such cases disc jockey shows are less expensive than other types of programs initiated by the local station. This is something which the CRTC will have to supervise closely.
Many of the disc jockey shows are loaded, and in the United States there have been pay-offs and kick-backs from record companies to disc jockeys, encouraging them to push particular records. This is something that must be borne in mind by the CRTC, as well as the time devoted to hot-line radio programs. If a controversy develops on a hot-line show, a station is inclined to devote a lot of time to that type of show to the exclusion of other forms of entertainment. This is particularly so in areas which are dependent on one radio outlet. There has to be a balance in these matters.
I appreciate the speed with which the government acted in this instance, Mr. Speaker. They have passed this legislation in advance of the United States and I know it is well received by radio stations and will make their operations easier and less expensive. The other fact has not been faced, however, and it involves the requests made by organizations representing actors, performers, artists and those connected with the production end of the recording industry. If any moneys are to be taken from the radio stations, obviously they should be directed to the performers.
It seems to me that we have an opportunity to encourage more Canadian talent now that the CRTC broadcasting regulations have been changed. We also have an obligation to provide the necessary funds in order to eliminate competition between the United States and
December 21, 1971

Canada so that it is not mandatory that anyone in this country seeking to rise above the current salary range look to the American market. Our market can be developed and more money provided to radio stations through the industry. I strongly urge the government to give the same speedy consideration to that aspect of the matter as was given to the protection of the radio stations who in my opinion were being victimized by an agency which found that the loopholes in the copyright legislation were almost a form of money.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, before this bill goes to the committee I would ask if a brief explanation is available. An explanation may have been given in the budget debate but I am not aware of it at the moment.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-261 provides for the implementation, without change, of the ways and means motion relating to the Customs Tariff which was tabled in the House on June 18. The clauses of the bill correspond to and are in the same order as the paragraphs of the ways and means motion.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) made mention of the more significant tariff changes which appear in the bill. These included the implementation of two Tariff Board reports without change. One proposed a reduced rate on raw materials used in the petrochemical industry, item 26910-1; the second recommended bringing the duties on polyethylene into line with the rates which apply on most other plastics made in Canada, items 93902-3, 93902-42 and 93902-82. He also referred to a new provision, item 41100-1, which would accord machinery used in sawmills and logging the same tariff relief as is now given to production machinery under the machinery program. Another change of general interest was removal of the duty on heavy fuel oils.
At this time I intend to comment only very briefly on the four clauses of the bill before the House. If hon. members so wish, I will be pleased to provide more detailed com-
Ways and Means
ments on individual tariff items of interest to them when we are going through the bill in committee of the whole.
The Customs Tariff contains three schedules. Schedule A to the Customs Tariff enumerates the goods subject to duty and those which enter free of duty. Schedule B provides for drawback of duty on certain products, while schedule C lists the goods which are prohibited importation.
Clause 1 of the bill amends schedule A to the Customs Tariff by deleting a number of existing tariff items and by inserting the tariff items which appear in schedule A to the bill. These changes are largely of a relieving or of a technical nature. They provide mainly for reduced rates of duty on production equipment and materials. They meet representations from associations and individuals.
Clause 2 of the bill deletes several items from schedule B to the Customs Tariff and provides for the insertion of the two items which appear on page 8 of the bill. Clause 3 provides for an amendment to an existing item in the prohibited schedule to the Customs Tariff. The amended wording is shown in schedule C to the bill. Finally, clause 4 is the usual provision for the tariff changes set out in the bill to come into force on a provisional basis on the day following the budget, subject to approval by Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the parliamentary secretary a question? What is meant by the expression "provides for drawback"? Is this an item which receives a rebate of excise moneys paid in the area of purchase and, if so, for how long a period does it apply?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A drawback is a refund that one is entitled to claim when goods have been imported under certain circumstances. The duty is paid in the original instance but if the party proves the necessary circumstances he is entitled to a refund.
For a year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall have to look at the bill, Mr. Speaker. I cannot say what time limit, if any, is imposed on the period for making application.

Mr. Speaker, in appropriate circumstances I think we might have some fun tonight. If I were endowed with the skills of the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and could write doggerel poetry, we could have a lot of fun looking through the various provisions that come up tonight for consideration in the Customs Tariff. The parliamentary secretary has read to us one of the most catholic, stereotyped statements ever to come out of the Department of Finance with regard to the customs section. I say "catholic" but I apologize and retract the term and say the most stereotyped statement.
Let us look at the various provisions. Some of them are worthy of note because they indicate an honest endeavour on the part of the government to do something, albeit belatedly, with regard to the petrochemical industry which has been in trouble for a long time. I recall my remarks in the budget debate of June in regard to the changes being made in the duties on petrochemical feedstock and other related provisions, and I still think that the government has given this industry a terrible knock

December^!, 1971
Ways and Means
on the head. This may be in expiation to some degree, but the proof of the pudding will be in the eating.
In his reply to these remarks I look to the parliamentary secretary to state what the reaction of the petrochemical industry had been to these changes, as it is now six months and three days since the tariffs were lowered. After all, they were effective on the night of June 18.
I return to my original theme. I am very sorry that my colleague from Halifax-East Hants is not here to assist me, because I think these changes would give his skills in doggerel verse unlimited scope. As I look at the first item I wonder, even though I know the government is able to escape payment of customs duties on its own purchases, whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is not trying to show industry and commerce how to decorate offices in the new style. The committee on miscellaneous estimates had something to say about the expenditure of $75,000 for imported tropical plants which were to be used in the new offices of the Minister of Finance. That minister is not bothered by any customs regulations, because the government of Canada can import any type of commodity free of customs duty. When we look at the first item under schedule A, item No 7801-1, what do we see? The item reads:
Palms, ferns, rubber plants (Ficus), cannas, dahlias, paeonias, rhododendrons including azaleas-
In British Columbia we put the accent on the first part of the word, not on the last.
I have never been sure how to pronounce that word correctly. I have always it pronounced it "azalea", with the German pronunciation.
That is not how it is pronounced in British Columbia.

All right, that is not how
it is pronounced in British Columbia. But in the country that grows these plants in great profusion, Belgium, the word is pronounced as I pronounced it. I have cousins living in a suburb of Antwerp, on Azalea Strasse. I shall stick to my ancestral pronunciation.
In British Columbia we call them azaleas.

The hon. member calls them azaleas his way. That is fine. But why is the change respecting azaleas in there? Is the plant included because it has become a favourite of the Minister of Finance and is to be used for purposes of office decoration? If so, he should be emulated across the country. I have dealt with the first item. The second item will bring me benefits. I have a reputation among my colleagues as being somewhat of a gardener, and I like it.
Hear, hear!

So for greater clarity may I say that gladiolus bulbs may be imported into the country as corms, duty free. I will take advantage of this item because I love gladiolus and I am grateful for this change. Then we come to item 7804-1, which has been

changed. It covers hydrangeas and other pot-grown plants.
Male or female?

Are we to go into a pot growing campaign for the growing of pot? I don't know. Mr. Speaker, listen to what it says at the end of that item:
All the foregoing imported or purchased in bond in Canada by florists or nurserymen for bona fide forcing-
What interest has the government in bona fide forcing? I know the government tries to force things through the House, but that is not bona fide forcing. What is bona fide forcing with regard to hydrangeas and other pot-grown plants? Those are some of the things we are concerned about in these changes in Bill C-261.
Then I turn to item 7915-1, which covers flowers and foliage, natural, cut, whether or not in designs or bouquets and-listen to this-"whether or not coloured by osmosis, not otherwise provided for." There is a tariff change in regard to that item.
And it must be put through before Christmas.

The next item I shall deal with is 19947-1. I invite hon. members who know the English language to tell me what "macerated paper pads" are. What does "macerated" mean? I do not know. Whatever it means, macerated paper pads must be terribly important because they are "for use exclusively in the packaging of fresh fruit". They are to be admitted to Canada duty free.
The next item I refer to is 23800-1, rice hulls. I do not know about this. I suppose, since this is such a "hull" of a government, this item appeals to them. In any event, they are to be admitted free of duty. Next I come to something serious. The queries I put to the parliamentary secretary originally were serious. I am referring to the reduction from three-quarters of one cent per gallon to one-third of a cent per gallon. Why the government has to hang on to that one-third of one cent, I do not know. Does it want to help the petrochemical industry?
I see sitting across from me the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) who represents the constituency of Verdun. I am interested in that constituency because I have acquired a daughter-in-law who is in the minister's constituency.
A daughter-in-law won or lost?

Round, and that caused grave problems within the industry. Then about 18 months ago Canada decided to float its dollar. This immediately caused an 8 per cent increase in the export price of petrochemicals and chemical derivatives from Canada. These commodities are sold in highly competitive world markets.
I see the Minister of Labour before me. Behind him sits the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) and the Minister of State responsible for information in Toronto.
He is not here.

My city of Edmonton is much concerned about the petrochemical industry; and may I say here that the Liberal member for one constituency in Edmonton in which is situated about 90 per cent of the petrochemical industry of the area has failed to appear in this House since September 6. This is the degree of interest the hon. member shows in the Parliament of Canada and representations made on behalf of his constituents.
He is looking after his constituents.
He is, like blazes, looking after his constituents. All I say is that this is a measure-
How do you know he hasn't been sick?

Sick? He is sick in his mind if, as a member of this House, he does not appear here. He looks after his personal business. He says that he refunds part of his salary. He was never elected a Member of Parliament to refund his salary to the treasury in whatever measure he does.
Be charitable. After all, it is the Christmas season.

I feel as charitable this evening as this bill does in so far as the petrochemical industry is concerned. It gives minute quantities, less than crumbs, to an industry that has had to lay off hundreds of highly skilled people. At least 80 per cent of this industry's production goes to the export markets. The government has draped this industry over a sawhorse and has proceeded to belabour, knock and expose it to the forces and the whims of world markets and world conditions as a sacrificial lamb.
I appeal to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. One of the particular skills Which we developed in our western universities was gained by people who today are walking the streets. The minister can shrug his shoulders. Many of my contemporaries at universities of western Canada, including my own University of Alberta, in Edmonton, and many younger than I went into the petrochemical industry as chemical engineers. Others, as we expected, obtained lucrative jobs. Today they are seeking employment. Why? Because this government, in a terribly misguided policy with regard to that industry, which was one of the aces we had up our sleeve, one of the bright hopes for Canada to compete in the world market, cut if
Ways and Means
off not only at the ankles but at the knees. They have now given it the knife at the throat.
This is the answer, a paltry cutback of petrochemical feedstocks that are imported into this country. As far as the Alberta petrochemical industry is concerned, this is meaningless because we do not import any feedstock. It is domestically produced. For the petrochemical feedstock producers in this country, this does not mean a thing. I would like the Minister of Labour to speak to his colleagues-
Not tonight.

No, not here. I would like them to "get with it" on this tragic situation that faces the petrochemical industry in this country. It does not necessarily employ hundreds of thousands or twenties of thousands of people. However, this industry represents thousands of highly skilled people, including their sales organizations. This government's answer to the competitive situation facing this industry from world forces is to further create difficulties. All I can say is that items 26906-1 and 26910-1, particularly the latter which only goes for a limited period, are frankly of little assistance compared to the problems they are facing.
I now turn to item 41098. This item has its origin in spraying and dusting machines and attachments therefor. It moves over to pruning hooks, pruning shears and dehorning instruments. That is a long way from spraying and dusting machines. Now we are going to admit duty free, electric bird-scaring devices but not including recorders. They have to be bona fide. They do not include recorders or reproducers using magnetic tape as a recording medium.
We do not want any stuffed bird-scarers.
What is an electric birdscaring device that does not use a tape? You may have some sort of a raucous artificial noise, but you cannot have a bird call or bird-scaring device on a tape.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why bother with a device? Just get the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). He will scare away any bird.

I wonder how the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) will interpret this. Some of his colleagues in the cabinet might be substituted for some of these things. Remember this, they are to be used exclusively for scaring birds by producing sounds simulating their natural alarm cries. In this period of an election we can expect all sorts of sounds to come from cabinet ministers. They will not only scare birds; they will scare small children and maiden ladies. Of all things, electric bird-scaring devices are to be admitted duty free into this country.
You should all have one.
And this has to be done before Christmas.

Yes, this has to be done before Christmas. I ask the little clutter of three ministers opposite who in Hades made these representations.

December 21, 1971
Ways and Means
The birdwatchers.
Under no circumstances would it have been the birdwatchers, because this would scare the birds.
Yes, away from the airports.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member has specifically asked, this particular item was requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I am sure they will be interested in his remarks.

That is fine. But the fact that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture requested it and the parliamentary secretary sententiously informed us of this particular point, I am wondering what on earth is its purpose. After all, if we wanted bird-scaring devices we would just trot out some of the cabinet ministers and parliamentary secretaries. They would even scare the crows from barbed wire fences.
There is one further item which affects the logging industry in British Columbia. The Machinery Advisory Board is now to be given power to advise the cabinet to remit duty on certain types of machinery used for the sawing of lumber and other operations in the logging industry. This is just to allow a little flexibility in particular cases. I would remind hon. members that at the time the Machinery Advisory Board was set up I drew attention to some of the difficulties which could arise through giving the board power to counsel the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to cause an Order in Council to be passed exempting a particular type of machine from duty. This lends itself to a particular type of representation.
I have had experience in the administration of customs duties. I was very privileged to work under a minister who sought to repel every type of personal pressure. He always said this was an area in which the sausage-slicing machine would operate. It would operate first on one slice of the sausage, then on the next and then on the next. If a minister were to allow relaxation in one particular area he could not easily resist further pressures from friends of the government. The taxpayers of this country are extremely adept at smelling out friends of the government. These people appear regularly with their advocates.
Wait till we get our turn.

Yes, you will have your friends and you will act in the same way. That is why I find your stand on these occasions is even more than hypocritical. It is sanctimonious. I say it is even more than sanctimonious. In any event, I have not heard hon. members of that party from logging constituencies speak on this item. They know what will happen. This will provide some help. It will help an industry which has been hard hit by the government's tax bill. It is going to get crumbs in return.
Then, again, will the parliamentary secretary tell me how many more times we shall be faced with item 440431? This item appeared on the list when I was a freshman member of this House and in every budget since then,

without fail, it has appeared as an extension. It has to do with certain types of aircraft which are prescribed by weight. The item does not include the engine. Mr. Speaker, no Minister of Finance, and I knew some very well, could ever give me a strict definition to cover this item or satisfactorily explain its appearance year after year.
If the government intends to help those producing small aircraft in this country, why do it on a year to year basis? Why not simply say it intends to protect producers of this type of aircraft, including or not including engines, depending on what the policy might be? This would apply to aircraft not exceeding a certain number of pounds, whatever the weight might be, and then they could leave us alone instead of asking us to approve this extension every blessed budget.
Then we come to item 44210-1:
Rotors, blade diaphragms, spindle discs, shafts and blades, wholly or in chief part of metal, of a class or kind not made in Canada, when imported for use by turbine manufacturers in the repair or remanufacture of gas or steam turbines and parts thereof entitled to entry under tariff item 42805-1.
We want an explanation of this item. The definition is a long one and there is no doubt a particular purpose in mind. Does this relate to a particular type of contract for aircraft repair? Does it relate to any defence sharing production agreement? I shall pass over the item which admits duty free the professional productions of artists when valued at not less than $75 each. Every genuine artist would be insulted if his productions were not valued at $75. Then there is reference to original paintings, seri-graphs and photographic or photo-mechanical representations, and so on, and an extension of free entry to hand-made appliques suitable only for use as wall hangings. Are these intended for the office of the Minister of Finance or for some other minister's office? They have to be produced by artists domiciled in Canada but residing temporarily abroad. What is the real reason for which we are asked to make this particular change?
There are two other items to which I should like to draw attention. In this modern day and age, in this modern culture, we shall now be able to import glass beads free of duty if they are hand-made articles. Does the "now generation" have to get special dispensation in order that the bead bands worn across their foreheads are brought in duty free?
The next item is 71115, which is pots or compressed pellets, but not of hash; these are made of peat.
Canadians, for the use of.

As a gardener I will benefit from those. These are for use exclusively in growing plants for transplanting purposes, or for protecting plants while growing. We shall have to pay 10 per cent duty on those. The last item I want to mention requires an interpretation. It is item 99208. I apologize to the House for making a little fun of the bill this evening, but this item under schedule C, to which reference is made in clause 3, relates to metallic trading checks in circular form-in other words, trading discs-"unless in any particular case or class of cases exempted from the provisions of this item by a regulation of the Governor in
December 21L 1971

Council". What on earth are we up to here? These metallic trading checks come under certain customs regulations and I suppose I could find them in the Customs Tariff.
I have one in my hand. It is round and metallic.

Incidentally, I see these round, metallic trading discs are prohibited goods; they cannot be imported. The Minister of Labour should put his away, if he has one, because they are prohibited. However, under this amendment the minister, as a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council, is asking us to deliberate on an Order in Council exempting them from this prohibition so they may be allowed in-perhaps in order to legitimize his possession of one. The Minister of Finance is now in the House and perhaps he would advise us why he is introducing this exception, and on the basis of the representations of whom? These metallic trading discs have been prohibited for some time, so why are they being allowed in now under an Order in Council?
My hon. friend from Halifax-East Hants, with his ability to write doggerel poetry, would have been in a far better position to give hon. members an entertaining dissertation this evening. I have gone through a list that I think frankly defies anybody's imagination. Outside of it being a sop to the petrochemical industry-and here the Minister of Finance has a good deal to answer for-and also offering some assistance of a questionable nature to the lumbering industry particularly of British Columbia, the rest of the bill simply adds bits and pieces of no consequence, yet we are being asked to pass it. We require an explanation, Mr. Speaker, either from the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary secretary.

Mr. Speaker, I do not have too much time this evening and perhaps I can do little more than congratulate my hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for his most interesting examination of the bill. When I first looked at it I thought it was a serious matter, but I have been dissuaded from that view having listened to his remarks. I always suspected that beneath that stern exterior dwelt a western Pagliacci, and we saw a great demonstration of that tonight.
I also thought that perhaps the censor who looked over this bill was like the censor looking at questionable pictures and literature as he carefully rolled over some of the salacious portions of the bill. It seems to me there are some ridiculous aspects to the bill, but I also think there are some serious matters in it and if I may call it ten o'clock I should like to discuss them on another occasion.

maintopic: FISHERIES-SELKIRK FISH PLANT-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE CLOSING
FISHERIES-SELKIRK FISH PLANT-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE CLOSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15 I asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) whether he could shed any light on the rumours that the Selkirk processing plant of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation would be closed. He replied, as reported at page 10491 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the 70-year old fish plant at Selkirk does not meet our standards for inspection. It is being phased out. However, we are hoping to develop new supplies of fish and to have a plant operating at Selkirk in the not too distant future.
I do not mind admitting that I am having a considerable amount of difficulty maintaining any degree of good temper and reasonableness in pursuing this question this evening. The first problem I had to deal with after my election to this House in the spring of 1970 was the location of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation's processing plant, whether it would remain in Selkirk or be located in a suburb of Winnipeg. During the months of May and June, 1970, the Minister of Fisheries and myself engaged in a number of exchanges on the subject in this House.
The question was, I then thought, finally resolved, in a manner not wholly unsatisfactory to myself and the people of the Interlake region but nevertheless in a way we could live with, when the minister on June 25, 1971, made the following statements during his reply to representations that I had made in an adjournment debate. The minister said at that time:
My own forecast now is that we will have at least two big processing plants in Manitoba. In other words, we will have one at Transcona and continue to have one at Selkirk.
Then he said:
We believe the plant now operating at Selkirk will be operating at or near capacity for a number of years to come.
Later he said:
My own forecast is that there will be two plants, an old one and a new one. The old one at Selkirk needs to be rehabilitated and this will take place beginning next year. I also expect employment in Selkirk will probably increase and not decrease in so far as fish processing is concerned.
Imagine, after having heard that kind of statement from the minister on the subject, my reaction, the reaction of the employees of the Freshwater Fish Processing Plant and the reaction of the people of the Interlake when it was announced by the FFMC last week that the Selkirk plant would cease to process fish within the month and close its doors entirely in five months, taking away from Selkirk in
10690

Dec ember 21,1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
the neighbourhood of 150 jobs. It was a reaction of shocked disbelief, succeeded by rage. After the assurances the minister had given us we felt, and justifiably in my opinion, that we had been betrayed.
Just a little more than a year after the minister had assured us that there would be two plants in Manitoba, one in Transcona and one in Selkirk, that the Selkirk plant would be refurbished and that employment in fish processing in Selkirk was more likely to increase than to decrease, it was announced that the plant would be closed. What circumstances have changed in the interim to make the FFMC and the minister change their minds? Local production of fish has not declined. Rather, it has gone up because when the minister made his statement, Lake Winnipeg was completely closed to fishing because of mercury pollution whereas now it is again being fished on a controlled basis. Moreover, at the time the minister made his statement, stocks of fish in Lake Winnipeg had been depleted due to overfishing, whereas now the stocks have had two years to begin a recovery.
When the minister made his statement in June, 1970, the prospect of a lucrative rough fish fishery was just a gleam in his eye, whereas only recently in this House he assured me, when replying to some remarks I had made about the need for an income support program for fishermen, that the investigations of his department into a rough fish fishery were progressing extremely well and held out the prospect of substantial employment in the future.
After looking at these facts one is hard-pressed not to believe that the minister's statement of June, 1970, was not simply designed to slap the lid on some extremely effective pressure being applied by residents of Selkirk and the Interlake. I am not about to suggest that the minister was a knowing party to deception, but I do know that if I was the minister and someone had given me information with which to reply to a parliamentary inquiry, and the reply I gave was afterwards demonstrated to be false, today I would be engaged in some head-hunting.
With that as background I wish to ask three very simple and direct questions to which the employees of the Selkirk processing plant, the citizens of Selkirk and the residents of Manitoba's Interlake are demanding answers. I hope the parliamentary secretary who will reply on behalf of the minister this evening will have the answers ready because they are obvious questions to ask. First, is it the intention of the minister to make the FFMC live up to the undertaking which he gave to me and to this House on June 25, 1970? Second, if he is not prepared to do that, why is he not prepared to do it? Third, if the best the people of Selkirk can now hope for is the new plant alluded to by the minister in his answer to my question on December 15, when will the construction of that plant begin, what will be its function, what will it cost and how many people will it employ?

speakeroldname: Mr. Eymard Corbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
maintopic: FISHERIES-SELKIRK FISH PLANT-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE CLOSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries has repeatedly stated his position regarding the Selkirk plant. He has, in the past, indicated to the House that his forecast was that the Selkirk plant could remain in operation after completion of the Transcona plant. How-

ever, the minister has never made a commitment to the effect that the Selkirk plant would never be closed down.
The operation of a fish processing plant in Selkirk remains possible. It hinges mainly on the development of a coarse fish industry, that is certain species which up to now had not been considered as being marketable.
During the summer of 1971, the federal fisheries service spent $413,000 on a research program directed toward improving the harvesting techniques used for coarse fish and, in the long run, the management of the production potential of Manitoba waters. This program, I might add, has employed 127 fishermen who would otherwise have remained idle. According to the data obtained, the potential of coarse fish seems promising. There remains a good number of problems to overcome particularly in relation to marketing. Research related to harvesting and processing will continue and the marketing aspect will be looked at with care. If all goes well a new plant in Selkirk could become economically feasible.
For now the Selkirk plant must close. With new inspection standards imposed on our American clients by their government, rehabilitation is not economically possible. We must accept that, after some 70 years of existence, that plant has become a victim of obsolescence. The new plant is Transcona takes over. Because the two plants are a mere 30 minutes away from each other by car, all employees of Selkirk have been offered jobs in Transcona. A good number of them have accepted this offer. They have received adequate training in the use of new techniques implemented in Transcona. The training program was carried out at no loss of income for the employees.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the government to date has improved fish processing, worked to put on a sounder base the management of Manitoba's fish resources, researched the possibility of creating a new industry with coarse fish, and protected the jobs of the Selkirk employees as much as possible. The establishment of a new plant in Selkirk will depend on the results of studies relating to the coarse fish industry. These studies are already under way and partly completed.

maintopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-WRITING OF EVALUATION REPORT BY PRIVATE CONSULTING FIRM-SELECTION OF PROJECT FOR ANALYSIS
YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-WRITING OF EVALUATION REPORT BY PRIVATE CONSULTING FIRM-SELECTION OF PROJECT FOR ANALYSIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 9 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) two questions regarding the evaluation report relating to the Opportunities for Youth program. The first question was:
In view of the fact that the evaluation report on the Opportunities for Youth program recently tabled in the House was carried out by a departmental task force, would the minister inform the House why the report itself was written by a private consulting firm?
Then I asked the minister the following supplementary question:
Would the Secretary of State inform the House how the sample of 356 projects analysed in the report was selected by his departmental task force?
December 21, 1971

I considered the reply that I received at that time from the minister to be inadequate partly because the report itself was long overdue. If you go through Hansard you will find the minister promised that the report would be ready by the beginning or the middle of October. On September 9, for example, he said in answer to a question in the House that in all likelihood the report would be ready at the beginning or the middle of October. On September 30, in answer to a question that I put to him, he said:
I estimated the assessment report on the project would be ready by mid-October, and I do not think there will be any considerable delay.
On November 22, when the report still had not been received, he said in answer to a question:
As for the report, I apologize to the House for the delay in tabling it, but this is a matter of data processing and the task force responsible for producing the report is working very hard at this . . . sand was hoping to be able to table this report as soon as possible.
We have had the report since the first part of December and in it we find that the conclusion is a glowing analysis of what happened to the Opportunities for Youth program and that things had gone very well indeed. Another reason I am not satisfied with the answer given by the minister, besides the fact that the report was long overdue, is that I question the validity of the report itself due to the fact that the analysis and evaluation are based on only a sample of all the projects in the country. And the minister said he did not know what kind of sample it was. We do not find anywhere in the report an indication of what sort of sample the evaluation is based upon. We have to know this if we are to know what type of credence to give to this evaluation of the Opportunities for Youth program.
We know that some months ago the department established a task force to evaluate Opportunities for Youth projects across the country, and after a period of several months of work it was decided that its report should be written by an outside consultant group called Systems Research Group Inc. They wrote the report on the basis of the data gathered by the task force established by the Department of the Secretary of State.
I want to know why the government decided to hire this firm after all the research had been done by the department itself. Was it because the task force members could not agree on the conclusions they were receiving from their research? Was this the reason that they called in an outside consultant firm to write the evaluation report itself? I think the long delay in presenting the report to the House lends credence to this possibility, because the report itself could have been written in two or three days once all the data had been gathered. It is only about 25 pages long. I think that an outside group writing a report for a government department should also do all the research and data processing. These are some of the reasons some of us are concerned that an outside group was called in to write the report.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I want to know how the sample of projects was chosen. Nowhere in the report does it say how the 300-odd projects were chosen, whether they con-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
stituted a representative sample, a random sample or what have you. The last sentence in the report reads:
In terms of the programs explicit objectives and within its budgetary constraints, OFY appears to have been very successful in the light of information now available.
What do they mean by "in the light of the information now available"? What information? This is what we must know if we are to judge this report on its merits. I think that any firm which had regard for its reputation would include a phrase like "on the basis of the information now available." I ask again, what kind of sample was it? Was it a representative sample, or was it not? You could make a report sound any way you wanted it to, if you carefully selected 300-odd projects out of the entire summer's program. Next year's program, it is hoped, will be announced by January 15, and before the end of this month we are to have a more thorough evaluation report on last year's program.
Many of the ideas in the Opportunities for Youth program are exciting. I hope that before next year's program is introduced we can clear up a few of the questions that I have tried to raise tonight, so that we will have a clear evaluation of last year's program. What type of sample formed the basis of the evaluation? Why was an outside firm brought in to write the report after the data had been gathered by a task force working within the department?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-WRITING OF EVALUATION REPORT BY PRIVATE CONSULTING FIRM-SELECTION OF PROJECT FOR ANALYSIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will make my answer very brief. The hon. member has put two questions before the House. In both instances he requested that they be given special consideration during the adjournment debate. The one he has dealt with this evening concerns the reason why an outside group of consultants was chosen to compile the results of the evaluation study of the Opportunities for Youth program, and he also inquired about how the sample was chosen.
His other question, while on the same subject, was directed to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and had to do with whether or not a special committee or a standing committee on youth and youth problems would be established and, if such a committee would not be established, whether the question of youth and youth employment would be referred to one of the standing committees.
Both questions touch on the general matter of the problems of youth, the special problems of the young people of this country and what the government is doing about them. These bear directly on the functions of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who is responsible for the Opportunities for Youth program. The questions the hon. member has asked are legitimate ones, but at the same time, bearing in mind the length of time and the terms of reference of last year's program, we all know now that some of the difficulties we experienced last year in the Opportunities for Youth program arose as a result of the rather foreshortened time period in which the program was put together.
The hon. member has made reference to the fact that the program for next summer is being prepared now. We think this is an improvement as it will give us an opportunity to get ready in plenty of time, and will also give members of this chamber a full opportunity to ask their

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
questions now rather than being caught as we were last year with the program being rushed into effect before members of the opposition had an opportunity to examine it.
I want to assure the hon. member and others here that through the regular parliamentary devices in committee, the estimates of the Secretary of State as they go to the standing committee when we return after the Christmas break in the ordinary course, in regard to any legislation that would have to be tabled and any other opportunities that hon. members have to put questions to the Secretary of State through oral questions, written questions on the order paper or perhaps through the use of allotted days if
the opposition sees fit, we hope hon. members will be reassured.
There will be many opportunities to question the Secretary of State about all these things and the plans that are going to be put into effect for next year's program so we can be sure to have a clearer understanding of it in view of our experience last year. The use of an outside group was hardly necessary and perhaps next year when the evaluation is done, and now that we have gained the experience, we will not need such a group. I conclude by saying that I hope the hon. member will take advantage of all these opportunities to ask questions about this matter as we develop next year's program.
